lead.headline: UN inquiry says Israel kept committing genocide in Gaza after ceasefire
lead.dek: A UN-mandated commission says Israeli forces continued genocidal acts after the October 2025 truce; Israel calls the report a misinformation campaign.
body: A UN-mandated Commission of Inquiry on the Occupied Palestinian Territory said on Monday that Israel kept committing genocide in Gaza even after the US-brokered ceasefire took hold in October 2025. In a report covering violations from 7 October 2023 to September 2026, the commission said Israel was committing "genocidal acts with the genocidal intent to destroy" Palestinians in Gaza, according to Reuters. The panel also accused Israel of crimes against humanity in the occupied West Bank.

The report describes a ceasefire that did not stop the violence. Israeli forces kept using heavy munitions, drones, artillery and sniper fire in densely populated areas, Reuters reported, while the so-called Yellow Line moved deeper into Gaza and hardened into a de facto border. The Associated Press said Israel's control of the territory grew from 53 percent to at least 60 percent since the truce, and that Israeli fire killed at least 196 Palestinians in that period, including 18 women, 32 boys and 11 girls. Palestinian authorities say more than 74,000 people have been killed in Gaza since 7 October 2023.

On the West Bank, the commission said Israeli soldiers and prison guards committed war crimes and crimes against humanity, including extermination, torture, rape and persecution. It counted 254 deaths from airstrikes between 7 October 2023 and 30 September 2026, against six in the 15 years before the war, and said displacement since January 2025 is the largest there since 1967, with 34,176 Palestinians still displaced as of August. AP reported six recent cases of Israeli guards sexually abusing male detainees from Gaza at the Sde Teiman military prison, and noted it could not independently corroborate several of the graphic accounts. The commission also faulted the Palestinian Authority for targeting dissenting Palestinians.

Israel's mission in Geneva rejected the findings, calling the report part of a misinformation campaign to demonise the country and calling for the commission to be dissolved. Israeli ambassador Daniel Meron said such efforts undermine Israel's legitimacy, and the mission urged the international community to repudiate the report. Israel has long denied the genocide and sexual-assault allegations. The commission's chair, Srinivasan Muralidhar, said the killings and home demolitions in the West Bank were part of a wider strategy to displace Palestinians.

The report now goes to the UN General Assembly. AP noted that its findings could be used by International Criminal Court prosecutors or in other jurisdictions seeking accountability. The commission's previous report, in September 2025, also concluded that genocide was taking place and said Israeli leaders had incited it, an accusation Israel called scandalous.
lead.why: The finding that a ceasefire has not ended alleged genocidal conduct raises the legal and diplomatic pressure on Israel and its allies, and it feeds directly into possible court cases.

more.headline: UN inquiry: Russia's strikes on Ukraine's energy grid are crimes against humanity
more.dek: A UN commission told the General Assembly that Russia's systematic bombardment of power infrastructure amounts to a crime against humanity.
body: The UN Independent International Commission of Inquiry on Ukraine submitted a report to the General Assembly this week concluding that Russia's systematic bombardment of Ukraine's energy infrastructure amounts to a crime against humanity. According to Democracy Now!, commission chair Pablo de Greiff said attacks that target civilian objects indispensable to the civilian population are unlawful and amount to war crimes, and the report finds Russian officials committed war crimes by directing attacks at civilian targets.

The findings landed as the strikes continued. Just Security's daily roundup, citing the New York Times, reported that a Russian attack hit Kyiv's Southern Bridge and subway infrastructure. Democracy Now! said Russia launched hundreds of drones and ballistic missiles across Ukraine overnight, killing at least one person and injuring 15 in Kyiv, including students in a dormitory.

Ukraine's air defence is also under strain. Just Security reported that President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Ukraine had waited nearly a month for US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth to allow missiles for its air defence systems to be sent. Moscow has not accepted the commission's findings in the sources reviewed for this edition.
more.why: A formal UN finding of crimes against humanity over attacks on power grids adds a legal basis for future accountability efforts as winter approaches.

more.headline: Anthropic files for Nasdaq listing, reporting $16.3 billion in half-year revenue
more.dek: The AI company filed its S-1 on Monday for a listing under the ticker ANT, disclosing fast growth, huge compute commitments and a large non-cash loss.
body: Anthropic filed a Form S-1 with the US Securities and Exchange Commission on Monday, setting up an initial public offering of Class A shares on Nasdaq under the ticker ANT. The price range and share count were left blank. Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley lead a group of about 22 banks, according to The Next Web and IPOScoop.

The filing says revenue for the first half of 2026 was $16.3 billion, up from $1.16 billion a year earlier. Second-quarter revenue was $11.6 billion, with a first operating profit of $974 million, though the half-year operating result was a $693 million loss. The net loss for the half was $80.7 billion, mostly a $72.4 billion non-cash charge from revaluing convertible notes. More than 11,900 customers pay at least $100,000 a year.

Timing and size are still reports rather than facts. The Wall Street Journal, cited by The Next Web, said Anthropic aims to list the week of 16 November at a valuation of $1.5 trillion to $2 trillion; Bloomberg, cited by IPOScoop, said marketing could begin the week of 9 November; Reuters reported a market value around $1.5 trillion.

The prospectus also lists risks, including an FTC civil investigative demand, a $1.5 billion copyright settlement, and warnings that losses from an AI catastrophe could exceed insurance capacity. Seven co-founders would hold a share carrying 50.1 percent of votes on ordinary matters. Disclosure: Weekfold's editions are drafted with the help of Claude, which Anthropic makes.
more.why: A listing of this size would be among the largest ever and would turn a private AI lab into a company whose finances and risks are public.

lead.headline: Israel's election ends with no clear winner as Arab parties surge
lead.dek: Netanyahu's bloc led but fell short of a majority, with record turnout and an unprecedented showing for Arab parties.
body: Israelis voted on Tuesday in their first general election since the 7 October 2023 attacks and the war in Gaza, and the result left neither side with a majority. With more than 85 percent of ballots counted, AFP reported that Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's bloc was on track for 53 of the 120 Knesset seats, former army chief Gadi Eisenkot's opposition alliance for 48, and Arab parties for 19. A coalition needs 61. Al Jazeera, working from an earlier count, put the bloc at 54 seats and reported that turnout of 77.7 percent was the highest since 1999.

Both camps claimed momentum. Eisenkot said the result would be "a new start", while Netanyahu said Likud was the largest party and called for a national right-wing government. Likud later accused the Arab lists of having stolen the election, alleging corruption and threats, but gave no evidence. Netanyahu has also called the idea of relying on Arab parties a disgrace.

The Arab parties are now kingmakers in all but name. Yair Golan, a leading opposition figure, called for an alliance with Arab lawmakers, while Joint List leader Yousef Jabareen said anyone seeking a real alternative to Netanyahu would have to talk to his party, though he told AFP it would not join a coalition outright. Eisenkot has ruled out serving with Netanyahu.

President Isaac Herzog urged parties to do everything to avoid another election, and he is reportedly backing a unity government. He will consult party leaders and name a candidate, who then has up to 42 days to assemble a coalition. If that fails, Israel heads back to the polls. Netanyahu stays on as caretaker prime minister in the meantime, and Al Jazeera said official results are due on 4 November.
The vote also unfolds against the war with Iran. AFP noted that Netanyahu ordered two campaigns against Iran, and that Trump has said Washington will not attack again until after the US midterms.
lead.why: A hung Knesset means weeks of coalition bargaining, possible new elections, and a government whose makeup will shape Israel's Gaza and Iran policy.

more.headline: Congo's Ebola outbreak passes 10,000 confirmed cases
more.dek: The Bundibugyo outbreak is now Congo's largest ever and the second-largest on record, with cases reported in Kenya and Nigeria.
body: Confirmed Ebola cases in the Democratic Republic of Congo rose above 10,000 on Tuesday, according to government data cited by Ghanamma. Congo's public health institute put the toll at 10,060 cases and 4,887 deaths. The outbreak, caused by the rare Bundibugyo species and announced in mid-May, is now the largest and deadliest in Congo's history, surpassing the 2018-2020 epidemic.

It is also the second-largest and second-deadliest Ebola outbreak on record, behind the 2014-2016 West African epidemic, which infected more than 28,600 people and killed more than 11,000. Kenya reported its first case earlier this month and has announced nine in total, including a man who travelled from Congo via Uganda and died in Nairobi. Last week Nigeria became the fourth African country to report a case. A Swiss diplomat's wife who had not travelled to Congo was flown home on Monday, and Switzerland believes she was infected in Uganda. Uganda says it has no cases now and will quarantine returning citizens for 21 days.

Democracy Now! reported that youths armed with machetes attacked two community health workers who were raising Ebola awareness in Congo, killing one and wounding the other. A UN spokesperson said such incidents show how violence and mistrust can undermine the response.
more.why: Spread beyond Congo and attacks on health workers suggest the outbreak is outpacing containment efforts.

more.headline: Rays beat Brewers 4-3 in 12 innings, force Game 5
more.dek: Tampa Bay stayed alive after trailing three games to none, winning on a chopper over first base after a Milwaukee error.
body: The Tampa Bay Rays avoided a World Series sweep on Tuesday night, beating the Milwaukee Brewers 4-3 in 12 innings at Tropicana Field in St. Petersburg, Florida, to force a fifth game, according to the Associated Press. Milwaukee had come within one win of its first championship after routing the Rays 10-1 in the previous game.

Milwaukee's Cooper Pratt hit a tiebreaking home run off Ian Seymour in the top of the 12th. The bottom half unravelled after third baseman Joey Ortiz made a throwing error on Junior Caminero's leadoff grounder. Liam Hicks singled, and Jonny DeLuca's single to centre scored pinch-runner Cedric Mullins to tie the game at 3. Chandler Simpson then loaded the bases, and with Milwaukee in a five-man infield, Ben Williamson, who was 1 for 15 in the postseason, chopped a ball over first baseman Jake Bauers into right field to win it.

Tampa Bay became the fifth of 26 teams to trail 3-0 in the World Series and win Game 4, and the previous four all lost Game 5. Of 43 teams to fall behind 3-0 in any best-of-seven postseason series, only the 2004 Boston Red Sox have come back to win. The Brewers (103-59) lead the series 3-1, and Game 5 was scheduled for Wednesday night at Tropicana Field with Milwaukee needing one win to clinch. This edition's sources do not cover the series result.
more.why: Even a 3-0 lead is not safe in baseball, and the Brewers' first title chase was extended by at least one more game.

lead.headline: High-speed train rams stopped train in Spain, killing at least 68
lead.dek: A state-run Renfe train struck the rear of a stopped Iryo train south of Madrid; the transport minister called the order to restart it inexplicable.
body: At least 68 people died on Wednesday morning when one high-speed train slammed into the back of another that was stopped on the tracks in central Spain, in the country's second deadly high-speed rail disaster this year. The collision happened at about 8:53 a.m. on the Madrid-Seville line in Toledo province, on a flat stretch between Urda and Los Yébenes, surrounded by olive fields. Two carriages derailed. The regional government of Castilla-La Mancha confirmed the toll, and 58 injured people were being treated in hospital, with AFP reporting that more than 100 were hurt and 15 were in a critical condition.

A train run by state-owned Renfe, carrying 397 passengers, hit a train of the private operator Iryo carrying 147. Transport Minister Óscar Puente said a safety system on a stretch of about 63 kilometres failed at 8:30 a.m. because of a computer malfunction, halting all trains there. Central command then told the Renfe train to restart without speed restrictions even though a stop signal remained active. He called the order inexplicable, said the drivers were not to blame, and said the train could have been travelling at close to 200 km/h. He added that he was not assigning responsibility to anyone and was only stating facts.

Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez, speaking at the site, announced three days of national mourning and said it was unacceptable for Spain to suffer two high-speed rail accidents in one year. King Felipe VI visited the scene, and European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said Europe mourned with Spain. The football federation postponed all 24 Copa del Rey games scheduled for the day, and the main Madrid-Andalusia line was suspended.

The crash echoes January's disaster near Adamuz in southern Spain, when an Iryo train derailed into an oncoming Renfe train and 46 people died. Before 2026, no fatal crash had occurred on Spain's dedicated high-speed lines since the network opened in 1992, AP noted. A union spokesperson said liberalisation of passenger services may not have been matched by upkeep of the lines, though he stopped short of calling it decisive.

Authorities are investigating, and the toll was expected to rise. Sánchez faces an early general election on 29 November, and both the Socialists and opposition leader Alberto Núñez Feijóo suspended campaigning.
lead.why: Two fatal high-speed crashes in ten months, one now blamed on a control-centre order, put Spain's rail safety and its rail liberalisation under intense scrutiny weeks before an election.

more.headline: Labor leader Dolores Huerta dies at 96
more.dek: The co-founder of the United Farm Workers, who coined "Sí se puede", died on Wednesday.
body: Dolores Huerta, the farmworker organiser and civil rights icon, died on Wednesday at the age of 96, Democracy Now! reported. Born in 1930, she co-founded the National Farm Workers Association in 1962 with Cesar Chavez; it later merged with the Filipino-led Agricultural Workers Organizing Committee to form the United Farm Workers of America. The union organised the Delano grape strike from 1965 to 1970, which ended in major gains for farmworkers' labor rights.

Huerta coined the slogan "¡Sí se puede!", which she has said she came up with in Arizona in 1972 during Chavez's 25-day water-only fast. She also worked in the women's movement and the immigrant rights movement and was a prominent supporter of the Democratic Party.

Her legacy took on a painful new dimension this year. After a New York Times investigation in March into Chavez's sexual abuse of women and girls in the farmworkers' movement, Huerta said Chavez had raped her in the 1960s and that the assaults led to the births of two of her children, whom she had kept secret. Journalist Maria Hinojosa, who interviewed her afterwards, described her as a perennial optimist who loved life and said Huerta told her she had been crying all morning when the story came out.
more.why: Huerta's life tied the farmworker movement to the wider fights for women's and immigrant rights, and her final public chapter forced a reckoning with the movement's own history.

more.headline: UN condemns US Cuba embargo as Washington expels Cuban diplomat
more.dek: The embargo vote passed with fewer supporters than last year, a day after a clash at the UN led to the diplomat's expulsion.
body: The UN General Assembly on Wednesday again voted to condemn the US economic embargo of Cuba, for the 34th year. Reuters, via Just Security, reported the tally as 130 in favour, 25 abstentions and 17 against, which is 35 fewer votes in favour than last year as more countries sided with Washington.

Cuban Foreign Minister Bruno Rodríguez Parrilla told the Assembly that the United States has openly threatened to use military force and imposed dozens of new coercive economic measures, according to Democracy Now!, which noted that the Trump administration has repeatedly threatened military intervention to change Cuba's political system and that Cuba has suffered outages, shortages and financial trouble. The embargo dates to 1960.

The vote followed a diplomatic rupture. The United States expelled Cuban UN Mission First Secretary Richard Tur de la Concepción after an altercation on Tuesday at the General Assembly with a US official. US Ambassador Mike Waltz posted video of the exchange, and the State Department said the diplomat was no longer welcome, the Wall Street Journal reported.
more.why: A shrinking majority against the embargo, alongside open US threats of force, shows Washington's pressure on Cuba is hardening.

lead.headline: Pentagon says Iran war has cost $47 billion as talks edge forward
lead.dek: The tally is up more than $3 billion in a month, while Vance and Gulf mediators try to revive negotiations before an expected US escalation after the midterms.
body: The Pentagon has told Congress that the US war on Iran has cost at least $47 billion, up more than $3 billion since last month, according to a US Central Command estimate reported by Democracy Now! and Al Jazeera. About $29 billion of the total is for replacing munitions. Foreign Exchanges, a daily newsletter, called the figure an underestimate. The administration is reportedly prepared to resume heavy attacks after next week's US midterm elections.

Diplomacy is moving in parallel. The Wall Street Journal reported that Vice President JD Vance sent a letter to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, to try to restart peace talks, at Trump's direction. Axios reported that Qatar-led mediators are working on a deal under which Iran would let UN inspectors into bombed nuclear sites in return for some sanctions relief. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araghchi said he was in close contact with mediators on a proposed seven-day plan to pave the way for reopening the Strait of Hormuz.

At sea, Iranian officials said three oil tankers caught fire after hitting mines while trying to cross the strait, and the Revolutionary Guards claimed four vessels were hit; neither claim was independently confirmed, and Central Command insists it has cleared the waterway. Democracy Now! said a tanker struck two weeks ago has left an oil slick more than 20 miles long and a spill has fouled beaches in northern parts of the United Arab Emirates.

The Wall Street Journal reported that Central Command chief Admiral Brad Cooper briefed Trump in person at the White House on military options. Just Security noted that US and Israeli officials say renewed bombing is likely soon after the midterms unless a last-minute deal emerges, and that South Korea is weighing options short of combat for a Hormuz deployment.

Also on Thursday, Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth fired Army Lt. Gen. Brett Sylvia, the Joint Staff's strategy and policy chief, without explanation, The Atlantic reported. Axios, cited by Foreign Exchanges, said Sylvia had reportedly admitted leaking classified information on Ukraine and Iran after failing polygraphs.
lead.why: The bill and the timetable show the war is on hold rather than over, with a decision on escalation tied to the US election calendar.

more.headline: Lagarde to leave the ECB in February, nine months early
more.dek: The European Central Bank president will step down on 7 February 2027, giving EU leaders time to pick a successor before French elections.
body: European Central Bank President Christine Lagarde announced on Thursday that she will step down on 7 February 2027, nine months before her eight-year term was due to end on 31 October 2027. The 70-year-old said in a short video that she leaves with a sense of good work done and an ECB fit for the future, according to Reuters and the Associated Press.

The timing is political. Her early exit lets EU leaders choose a successor before the French presidential election in spring 2027, which polls suggest Marine Le Pen is favoured to win. EU Council President Antonio Costa said the succession process would start immediately. Reuters named Dutch former central bank head Klaas Knot and Spain's Pablo Hernández de Cos as frontrunners, and noted that Isabel Schnabel leaves the ECB's board in early January and Philip Lane's term ends in May, so the posts may be filled as a package. Berenberg's Holger Schmieding said leaders would likely aim to settle them before a summit on 17-18 December.

Markets barely reacted. The ECB held its deposit rate at 2.5 percent this week, signalling another rise could come in December, while bond yields, especially in France, are climbing. Jean-Philippe Tanguy, a senior Le Pen economic aide, said he saw it coming, while German MEP Markus Ferber said it sent the wrong signal.
more.why: Choosing the next head of the euro zone's central bank during a rate-hiking cycle and a French election run-up makes this one of Europe's most consequential appointments.

more.headline: Russian drone kills 13 at Dnipro station as Oleshky truce holds
more.dek: A rare local ceasefire arranged for the occupied town of Oleshky was holding, even as Russia struck a crowded railway platform.
body: A Russian drone hit a crowded platform at the main railway station in Dnipro on Thursday, killing at least 13 people, according to regional governor Oleksandr Hanzha as cited by Reuters; another roundup put the toll at 14. Ukrainian Railways said people were on the platform despite a warning of heightened danger. Moscow's mayor said Russia downed most of 613 drones heading toward the capital overnight.

Elsewhere on the front, a limited ceasefire around the Russian-occupied town of Oleshky in Kherson region was holding. The White House said First Lady Melania Trump helped broker it, and Russian General Valery Gerasimov said Russian forces would stop firing on the Kherson axis from 4 a.m. Moscow time on Tuesday so that aid could be delivered and civilians could leave. Oleshky had about 24,000 residents before Russia captured it in 2022 and has had no electricity, heat or running water, with mined roads and scarce food and medicine, AP reported. Estimates of how many people remain range from about 2,000 to 6,000. An aid shipment was due on Thursday.

The Wall Street Journal, cited by Foreign Exchanges, also reported that Ukraine stopped striking Russian oil refineries earlier this month after weeks of US pressure, a halt that may not last beyond the US midterms.
more.why: The strike shows civilian transport is still a target, while Oleshky is a test of whether small humanitarian truces can work in a war with no wider ceasefire.

lead.headline: Nasdaq has worst day since June on AI spending fears
lead.dek: Intel plunged nearly 29 percent and chip stocks tumbled, leaving the Nasdaq down 5.3 percent for October.
body: Wall Street closed sharply lower on Friday as worries about the cost of the artificial-intelligence build-out sparked a broad sell-off in technology shares. The Nasdaq Composite fell 2.86 percent, or 747.73 points, to 25,437.00, its biggest one-day percentage drop since 5 June, according to Reuters. The S&P 500 lost 1.82 percent to 7,580.07 and the Dow Jones Industrial Average fell 1.09 percent to 51,770.31. The Nasdaq now sits 7.8 percent below its record close of 6 October.

Intel led the rout, dropping 28.6 percent after disappointing quarterly results released late Thursday. Yahoo Finance reported that chief executive Lip-Bu Tan blamed a PC slowdown linked to memory prices and availability. Nvidia fell 4.2 percent, AMD 10.9 percent, and the broader chip index 7.2 percent, leaving it down more than 15 percent for the month. Dell and HP fell about 11 and 10 percent. Crypto-linked stocks Coinbase, Strategy and Robinhood dropped between 7.2 and 10.6 percent after reports of a $6.3 billion hack at Binance.

For the month, the Nasdaq lost 5.3 percent, its worst month since March 2025, Yahoo Finance reported, while the S&P 500 fell about 1.2 percent and the Dow gained about 1.5 percent. Oil and energy shares ran the other way: Exxon Mobil rose 2.2 percent and Chevron 2.8 percent after beating profit forecasts, and US crude settled around $104 a barrel.

Investors were also reading the Federal Reserve. Yahoo Finance reported that two Fed officials, St. Louis Fed president Alberto Musalem and Richmond Fed president Tom Barkin, said rates may need to go higher after the Fed held steady in a split vote this week. Oliver Pursche of Wealthspire Advisors told Reuters: "Those that are falling short are getting punished."

Earnings overall have been strong. Reuters said 82 percent of the 299 S&P 500 companies that have reported beat estimates. Truist's chief investment officer, Keith Lerner, said tech could have downside of roughly 2 to 8 percent from here, while noting that the S&P 500 is still up about 111 percent since October 2022.
lead.why: The sell-off shows how much of the market's value now rests on AI spending paying off, and how quickly confidence can turn when a bellwether disappoints.

more.headline: Binance says $6.3 billion stolen in the biggest crypto heist on record
more.dek: Analysts blame a North Korean unit; about $3 billion was frozen and the exchange says it will cover users' losses.
body: Binance said about $6.3 billion in crypto was stolen from the exchange, which appears to be the largest crypto theft ever. Al Jazeera noted the previous record was the roughly $1.5 billion taken from Bybit in February 2025. TRM Labs and Chainalysis say most of the theft occurred over about 20 minutes starting late Thursday. The exchange suspended deposits and withdrawals, and founder Changpeng Zhao said on X that it had likely been hacked, TechCrunch reported.

Reuters, cited by Al Jazeera, said about $3 billion has been frozen, including more than $2.3 billion by stablecoin issuers Tether and Circle; Binance has not said where the other $3.3 billion went. TRM said with high confidence that TraderTraitor, a North Korean unit linked to the Lazarus Group, carried out the attack, and Chainalysis reached the same conclusion. North Korea routinely denies such claims. Binance co-CEO Richard Teng said the investigation had not attributed responsibility to any individual.

Binance says user funds are safe and that it will cover all losses. It first said the breach might have started with a hacked engineer's laptop, then cited additional points of breach, and said it found no evidence that a wallet private key leaked. It said it is on track to resume withdrawals within 45 hours. Bitcoin touched a six-week low of about $76,368, and Coinbase, which said it was unaffected, fell 4.8 percent.
more.why: A theft of this size, attributed to a state-linked hacking unit, tests how well exchanges protect customer money and how fast stablecoin issuers can freeze stolen funds.

more.headline: NASA asks industry how to boost, service or retire the Hubble telescope
more.dek: A request for information issued Thursday seeks commercial options to extend Hubble's life before its orbit decays.
body: NASA issued a request for information on 29 October asking companies how they could service the Hubble Space Telescope, which has no propulsion and is slowly sinking as atmospheric drag lowers its orbit. The request is not a contract award. It covers three options: a mission to boost Hubble to a higher altitude, servicing to enhance its capabilities, or a controlled re-entry or disposal at the end of its life. Responses are due at 3 p.m. EST on 30 November.

NASA's analysis predicts Hubble would re-enter around 2033 to 2034 if left alone, and the agency expects any rescue mission would need to fly by 2032. NASA Administrator Jared Isaacman said extending Hubble's life would mean more discoveries and more science, and Nicky Fox, head of the Science Mission Directorate, said the agency is eager to explore the possibilities. Fox also referred to a flagship mission to follow Hubble.

Hubble, launched in 1990, was last repaired by astronauts in 2009 on the fifth shuttle servicing mission, which also installed a device meant to help a future spacecraft dock. Tech Times noted that NASA declined a private reboost proposal from Isaacman in 2024, before he became administrator.
more.why: Hubble is still producing science, and the request is the first sign NASA may accept outside help to keep it flying rather than let it fall.

lead.headline: Studies find global warming is accelerating, with seven climate records broken
lead.dek: Researchers say the warming rate has almost doubled over the past decade, and a separate annual report finds seven of 16 vital signs at record extremes.
body: Two studies published this month point to a planet warming faster than before. In Geophysical Research Letters, Grant Foster and Stefan Rahmstorf of the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research found that global temperatures have risen by about 0.35 degrees Celsius per decade over the past 10 years, nearly twice the just-under-0.2 degrees per decade seen from 1970 to 2015. ScienceDaily, which carried the institute's release, said the acceleration is statistically significant at more than 98 percent confidence.

The team analysed five major datasets, from NASA, NOAA, HadCRUT, Berkeley Earth and ERA5, after removing natural influences such as El Niño. Signs of acceleration appear in all five from around 2013 or 2014, and 2023 and 2024 remain the hottest years on record even after adjustment. If the past decade's rate continues, the researchers say, the 1.5 degree Paris Agreement limit could be exceeded on a long-term basis before 2030.

A separate report, the seventh annual State of the Climate analysis in the journal BioScience, looked at 16 planetary vital signs and found seven at record extremes: sea level, ocean heat content, glacier thickness, Greenland ice mass, and the three main greenhouse gases. Eos, the American Geophysical Union's news outlet, reported that carbon dioxide passed 428 parts per million in May 2026, about 50 percent above pre-industrial levels, and that the warming rate has roughly doubled from about 0.19 degrees per decade in 1970 to 2010 to about 0.36 since 2010.

There is some good news. The report says global oil, coal and gas use rose 0.9 percent in 2025, but renewables overtook coal in global electricity generation that year. Co-author William Ripple, of Oregon State University, warned that continued warming could trigger additional feedbacks and tipping points, including a slowdown of the Atlantic overturning circulation, Amazon dieback and ice-sheet melt in Greenland and West Antarctica.
The two analyses use slightly different baselines, which explains the small gaps in their decadal rates.
lead.why: If warming has indeed sped up, the window for limiting it to 1.5 degrees is closing faster than most plans assumed.

more.headline: Israeli attacks kill at least four in Gaza as truce frays
more.dek: More than a year into the ceasefire, Gaza's health ministry says at least 1,580 Palestinians have been killed since it began.
body: Israeli attacks killed at least four Palestinians in Gaza on Saturday despite a ceasefire that has been nominally in place for more than a year, Al Jazeera reported, citing Anadolu. Teacher Diaa Abu al-Rous was killed when Israeli shelling struck the Nuseirat refugee camp, al-Awda Hospital confirmed. Arafat al-Arair died of wounds from an earlier strike on a vehicle in Gaza City's Tel al-Hawa district, and two girls died when their tent caught fire at a displacement camp in al-Mawasi, Khan Younis; the cause of the fire was unclear.

Gaza's health ministry says at least six people were killed in the past 48 hours and 26 wounded, and that Israeli attacks have killed at least 1,580 Palestinians and injured 5,711 since the October 2025 ceasefire. Democracy Now! reported earlier in the week that a strike on the Ministry of Economy building in al-Mawasi killed four and wounded at least 15.

The UN human rights office warned on Friday that Israeli forces continue to displace Palestinians and raised concerns of ethnic cleansing as people are pushed into a shrinking area. Al Jazeera said the Israeli military is working to expand control of Gaza to 70 percent, following an order from Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu in May. Talks on a permanent end to the war under President Trump's plan have stalled: Hamas says it will not fully disarm until Israel withdraws, while Israel says it will not leave until Hamas gives up its weapons.
more.why: The steady toll shows how thin the ceasefire is and why the stalled peace plan matters for civilians.

lead.headline: Trump closes midterm campaign as record early voting tops 52 million
lead.dek: With Election Day on Tuesday, Republicans are defending a Senate majority, and courts are ruling on fights over ballots and voter checks.
body: President Donald Trump is wrapping up a turbulent midterm campaign with rallies in two states he has carried before: Iowa on Sunday afternoon, where Republicans are trying to hold a Senate seat and the governor's office, and Kansas on Tuesday, Election Day, according to the Associated Press. Trump cancelled and then abruptly rescheduled the stops as Republicans work to protect a Senate majority the AP described as at risk of slipping away. More than 52 million votes have already been cast.

AP reported that the elections are becoming a referendum on Trump's second term, with voters, including past supporters, questioning the economic fallout of his tariffs and of the war in Iran. In Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton is running a strong bid to become the state's first Democratic senator in 94 years. Democrats face their own problems in Michigan, where Senate nominee Abdul El-Sayed is feuding publicly with Rep. Haley Stevens. Senator Tim Scott, who chairs the Republican Senate campaign committee, said on NBC that Trump's agenda is on the ballot.

The legal fights are heating up. Just Security's roundup noted that a federal judge, David Carter, rejected the Justice Department's bid to force California to set aside 20,000 ballots from people it called likely noncitizens, saying it would disrupt an election already underway; the administration had also asked Washington state to set aside hundreds of ballots. A civil-rights group sued over a plan to send hundreds of investigators to find noncitizen voters.

In Alaska, the governor ordered a criminal investigation after the New York Times reported that Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola's campaign and party operatives recruited a second candidate named Dan Sullivan to confuse voters. Peltola and the Democratic Senate campaign committee deny the report, though a former campaign manager told the Times that Peltola knew of the plan.
Election Day is Tuesday 3 November.
